title: An Outcome-Based Educational Recommender System
extended_summary:
This paper addresses a major gap in educational recommender systems: most are evaluated using engagement-oriented metrics such as clicks, ratings, or retention, rather than whether they actually improve learning. The authors propose OBER (Outcome-Based Educational Recommender), a framework that embeds learning outcomes and assessment items directly into the recommender system’s data model so that recommendation methods can be judged on learner mastery rather than only on relevance or usage behavior.

The intervention is the OBER framework itself and its integration into NamazApp, a non-formal mobile e-learning application designed to help beginners learn Muslim prayer. OBER adds explicit Outcome entities, aligns learning items to outcomes, and computes mastery from interaction logs using assessment-linked items. The system is designed to be method-agnostic, and the authors tested three recommendation approaches within the same platform: a fixed expert-curated trajectory, collaborative filtering (CF), and knowledge-based (KB) filtering.

The study was conducted in an online non-formal learning setting with over 5,700 learners, with roughly 1,800 learners randomly assigned to each of the three conditions. Participants were end-users of NamazApp, treated here as learners/students in an adult non-academic context. The experiment lasted two weeks and used platform log data to compute three types of outcomes: retention, recommendation relevance via click-through rate, and outcome mastery based on assessment performance.

The main conclusion is that OBER makes it possible to compare recommender strategies on pedagogically meaningful outcomes without adding separate testing overhead. In the reported trial, collaborative filtering produced the highest retention, but the fixed expert-designed path achieved the highest mastery, while knowledge-based recommendations performed in between. The authors argue that optimizing for engagement alone does not guarantee better learning, and that outcome-based evaluation should be a first-class component of educational recommender systems, especially in non-formal settings.

identified_tools.name: OBER
identified_tools.description: An Outcome-Based Educational Recommender system that embeds learning outcomes and assessment items into an educational recommender data schema so recommendation methods can be evaluated by learner mastery as well as engagement metrics.
identified_tools.use_case: Integrated as an API service into the NamazApp mobile e-learning application to compare three recommendation methods—fixed expert trajectory, collaborative filtering, and knowledge-based filtering—over two weeks using retention, click-through rate, and outcome mastery derived from interaction logs.

findings.finding_summary: In a two-week online controlled A/B/C test in NamazApp, OBER enabled comparison of recommendation methods within one unified logging and mastery pipeline across 5,751 learners total (CF n=1856, Fixed n=1963, KB n=1932). The system produced comparable retention, relevance, and mastery metrics without separate testing phases, demonstrating embedded outcome measurement during normal usage.
findings.measure: Ability to compare recommendation methods using unified logging, CTR, retention, and mastery metrics in live deployment

findings.finding_summary: Across the OBER-mediated experiment, the fixed expert trajectory achieved the highest average total mastery score per learner (0.4641), followed by knowledge-based filtering (0.4212) and collaborative filtering (0.3899). The paper also reports that the fixed method showed the steepest mastery growth over the first ten sessions, indicating stronger learning outcomes than the personalized alternatives tested.
findings.measure: Average total mastery score per learner; mastery growth over first ten sessions

findings.finding_summary: Using OBER's shared evaluation framework, collaborative filtering showed the highest average retention (6.16 sessions per learner) and slightly highest click-through relevance (CTR=0.3033), compared with the fixed trajectory (retention=5.63, CTR=0.3026) and knowledge-based filtering (retention=5.02, CTR=0.3007). Thus, the framework surfaced a trade-off where the most engaging method was not the one with the highest mastery.
findings.measure: Average sessions per learner; average click-through rate for recommendations per learner
findings.effect_size: Retention: CF=6.16, Fixed=5.63, KB=5.02; CTR: CF=0.3033, Fixed=0.3026, KB=0.3007

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical online controlled experiment with random assignment across three live conditions and a large sample (over 5,700 learners), which is stronger than correlational work. However, the paper reports no significance tests, confidence intervals, or standardized effect sizes, so there are some credibility concerns.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows meaningful differences in mastery and retention across methods, but impact remains unclear because no inferential statistics or standardized effect sizes are reported. Reported outcome differences are descriptive rather than firmly quantified for causal magnitude.
